edges.description: The duplication alters the part of BCOR that binds PCGF1, and a BCOR fragment that carries it does not assemble with PCGF1. Shown with purified proteins.

A complex that cannot be built cannot silence its target genes. The link is proposed: the experiments show that the duplication derepresses polycomb targets and, separately, that it prevents assembly, and no experiment connects the two.
The released genes are proposed to transform a neural precursor. The steps between are not established, and the human cells in the experiment did not grow faster.
The growing tumour is the mass found in the brain.
The tumour returns after resection and can then spread. What makes it recur is not known.
A large mass raises the pressure inside the skull.
A tumour of the cerebellum disturbs balance and coordination.
A tumour of the cerebral cortex can cause seizures.

nodes.description: A short stretch of the last exon of BCOR is duplicated in tandem and in frame, on one allele. The duplication adds 9 to 42 amino acids, most often 20 to 30, near the end of the BCOR protein. It was found in all ten tumours of the defining class that were sequenced in 2016, and it is the same duplication as in clear cell sarcoma of kidney. It is a somatic change. The tumours express BCOR at high levels, which is why a mechanism other than simple loss of BCOR has been proposed. The cell in which the duplication arises is not settled: one study argues from gene expression for a primitive neuro-glial progenitor, and another from stem cell markers for a neuroepithelial stem cell. The cell type bound here is the first of these and is an inference.

nodes.description: In human neural stem cells, BCOR with the duplication released genes that polycomb complexes keep silent, compared with normal BCOR. nodes.description: BCOR is part of PRC1.1, a variant of polycomb repressive complex 1, and the complex is built through the binding of the PUFD domain of BCOR to PCGF1. The duplications of the kidney and brain tumours fall in the two ends of that domain, which form the binding surface. In binding experiments, a BCOR PUFD with a duplication failed to assemble with PCGF1, and the authors conclude that losing the ability to build PRC1.1 is the event that drives the tumours. Whether the complex is lost or altered in the tumour cells themselves has not been shown.
